27958.etyen:
Compound of jul (“Christmas”) + evangelium (“gospel”), with linking -e- (“interfix”), literally “Christmas gospel”.
The first element, jul (“Christmas”), is from Old Norse jól (“Yule, Christmas”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą (“Yule”) or *jeulō; its further origin is uncertain. The second element, evangelium (“gospel”), is from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”). Its εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) element ultimately continues Proto-Hellenic *ehu- (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”); the deeper origin of the ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”) element is unc

49718.etyen:

en.g: Kristiansund (a town and municipality of Møre og Romsdal, Western Norway, Norway)

1000758.etyen:
Kristian + sund, named after Christian VI of Denmark, the King of Denmark and Norway from 1730 to 1746, who gave the town township rights in 1742. The original spelling of the city was Christianssund, used from 1742 to 1877, then the spelling Kristianssund was used until 1889, and the modern spelling Kristiansund has been used since.
The town was referred to as Fosna or Fosen, before given township rights, from Old Norse fólgsn (“hiding place, hidden port”). It was also often named Lille Fosen ("the small Fosen") to distinguish it from the island Storfosna ("the big Fosen") in Ørland to the no

en.g: a female given name from Ancient Greek, equivalent to English Carina, chiefly a spelling variant of Karina

1001014.etyen:
A spelling variant of Karina, a newer form of Katrina, ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη (Aikaterínē, “female given name”). The original meaning is uncertain, though the name was early associated with καθαρός (katharós, “pure”). Alternatively, Carina may derive from the Latin name Cara, from the feminine form cara (“dear, beloved”) of carus (“dear, beloved”).
Compare Danish Carina and Swedish Carina (“female given name”).

en.g: a male given name from Old Norse

1001270.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Sveinn m, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”), from Proto-Germanic *swainaz (“relative, kinsman; young man; herder”). The deeper origin of the Proto-Germanic noun is uncertain. It may be connected with Proto-Indo-European *s(w)e- (“oneself; one's own; separate”), or alternatively with *swīną (“swine”), through an earlier meaning “swineherd”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Svein, Faroese Sveinur, Icelandic Sveinn, Danish Svend and Swedish Sven (“male given name”).

1002038.etyen: A short form of female given names ending in -rina, such as Katarina, Karina and Severina. Since these longer names may have different origins, Rina has no single ultimate etymology. First attested in the 1820s in Norway.

The first element Lærdal is from Middle Norwegian Lærdall, attested in 1427, from Old Norse Læradalr, probably reduced from reconstructed *Lærardalr. The latter consists of the genitive *Lærar of a lost river name *Lærr and dalr (“valley, dale”), literally “valley of the Lærr”. The river name *Lærr is of uncertain origin. en.g: a lake in Melhus municipality and Orkland municipality, Trøndelag, Norway, receiving the river Skolda and draining through Sagelva into Svorka

1004598.etyen:
From the compound stem Svork- of the river name Svorka and sjøen (“the lake”). The origin of Svorka is uncertain. Peter Andreas Munch connected the name group with a reconstructed Norwegian verb *svirka, corresponding to Proto-Germanic *swerkaną (“to become dark”), reflected in Old English sweorcan (“to become dark, be obscured”). If this explanation is correct, the river name would have meant approximately “the dark one”.
Compare the Norwegian river names Sorka, Surka, Svarka and Sverka.
